The district court also looked to the operating procedures governing 
the implementation of DACA, noting that they '‘contain[ ] nearly 150 pages 
of specific instructions for granting or denying deferred action” and involve 
the use of standardized forms for recording denials—a fact the majority 
mentions. But no such operating procedures for the implementation of 
DAPA appear in the record—a fact the majority does not mention. As noted 
above, the USCIS is currently “in the process of determining the procedures 
for reviewing requests under DAPA.” In any event, even “specific and 
detailed requirements” may qualify as a “ ‘general’ statement of policy.” 
Guardian Fed. Sav. & Loan Ass’n v. Fed. Sav. & Loan Ins. Corp., 589 F.2d 
658, 667 (D.C.Cir.l978). And the “purpose” of a statement of policy is to 
“channel discretion” of agency decision makers; such channeling does not 
trigger the requirements of notice-and-comment unless it is “so restrictive 
. .. that it effectively removes most, if not all, of the [agencyj’s discretion.” 
Prof Is & Patients, 56 F.3d at 600. As for the use of standardized forms to 
record denials, what matters is not whether DAPA decisions are 
memorialized in a mechanical fashion, but whether they are made in such 
a fashion. For the many reasons discussed above, the district court had no 
legitimate basis for concluding that they wiU be. * * *
No t e s
1. 
Aftermath. After the Fifth Circuit affirm a H the preliminary 
injunction, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in January 2016. Less than 
one month after the grant. Justice Scaha died. Reduced to eight Justices, the 
high court heard argument in the case but ultimately deadlocked 4-4 that 
June, affirming the Fifth Circuit’s judgment by default and issuing no opinions 
of its own. (The deadlock may have been on one or more merits questions, or 
on the question of the state plaintiffs’ constitutional standing, or all of the 
above.) President Trump took office in January 2017. In June of that year, DHS 
rescinded DAPA. Due to the preliminary injxmction, still in force at the time of 
rescission, no grants of deferred action under the program had ever been madA
2. 
Factual Disputes over Rigidity in the Application of Policy 
Statements. As you can see from the Fifth Circuit opinion and dissent, the 
question of whether an agency document that purports to be nonbinding on its 
face is actually binding when apphed to individual matters can involve a very 
complex factual dispute. In contrast to General Electric, which focused mainly 
on the document’s text and examined agency practice only briefly, Texas v. 
United States premises its holding largely on agency practice. The detail of the 
fact-finding and the controversy over it are unprecedented. After researching 
decades’ worth of case law in this area, the editors of this casebook are aware 
of only one other opmion in which an appellate court puts even close to so much 
weight on the rigidity of administrative practice (as compared to the usual 
focus on mandatory-sounding text) in finding a policy statement to be a 
legislative rule. U.S. Telephone Association v. FCC, 28 F.3d 1232, 1234-35 
(D.C. Cir. 1994).
